title: A sunspot looks black, but on its own it would shine brighter than the full Moon

cover.alt: The orange disc of the Sun in visible light, with a cluster of dark sunspots near its left edge.
cover.credit: NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center/SDO · Public domain

body: Sunspots are patches where bundled-up magnetic fields block the hot gas that normally wells up from inside the Sun, so the surface there cools from about 5,780 K to roughly **3,000–4,500 K**. That is still searingly hot: cut out and seen on its own, a single sunspot would shine brighter than the full Moon, glowing crimson-orange. It only looks black because the surface around it is so much brighter. Sunspots range from about 16 km to 160,000 km across, and the biggest can be seen without a telescope, through a proper solar filter.

slides.alt: Time-lapse of the orange Sun: a cluster of dark spots appears at its left edge, grows, drifts across its face and slips off the right edge, while a few small spots travel with it.
slides.caption: 17 to 29 October 2014: the Sun’s rotation carries AR 12192, the biggest sunspot group of its solar cycle up to then, across its face. NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory, sped up 2×.
slides.credit: NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center/SDO · Public domain · excerpt, cropped, sped up 2×

slides.prompt: The sunspot group took about two weeks to cross the Sun’s face. Why does it move at all?
slides.detail: The spots are part of the surface, so the Sun’s rotation carries them from one edge to the other. Sunspot counts even show a 27-day rhythm from this rotation.

It looks dark next to the brighter surface

slides.label: across: the biggest sunspots, more than 12 Earths wide
slides.text: The smallest are about 16 km wide. A sunspot can last anywhere from a few days to a few months before it decays.

slides.question: Who left the oldest known record of sunspots?
slides.explanation: The earliest record is in the Chinese I Ching, completed before 800 BC. The first telescope sightings came much later, in 1610.
